chunks.title: What counts as a secret and where it must NOT live
chunks.content:
What counts as a secret and where it must NOT live

A secret is any value whose disclosure compromises a system: passwords, API tokens, signing keys, TLS private keys, database credentials, JWT signing material, encryption keys. Secrets must never live in: Git repositories (even private), container images, environment-variable defaults, CI logs, error messages, application logs, or developer laptops in plain form. They must live in a system designed for secrets — with audit, access control, encryption at rest, and rotation.

Decision rules:
- STORE secrets only in: AWS Secrets Manager, AWS SSM Parameter Store (SecureString), HashiCorp Vault, or equivalent
- FETCH secrets at runtime via the workload's IAM identity (IRSA, instance profile, task role) — no static credentials in pods
- REDACT secrets in logs at the log shipper / OTel Collector — never trust applications to redact reliably
- AUDIT secret access — every read of a production secret must produce a CloudTrail or Vault audit record
- ROTATE on every personnel change with access — not just on a schedule

Trade-offs:
- Centralized secret store: single source of truth vs single dependency — design for high availability
- Short-lived dynamic secrets (Vault DB engine): best practice but requires Vault investment
- Encrypting at rest in Git (sops, sealed-secrets): convenient GitOps vs harder rotation, no audit on access

Anti-patterns:
- Secrets in environment variables baked into the Docker image at build time
- `kubectl create secret` from a developer laptop with the real value pasted on the CLI
- Logging the full request including Authorization headers
- Sharing the same DB password across dev/staging/prod

metadata.title: What counts as a secret and where it must NOT live

chunks.title: When to choose AWS Secrets Manager vs SSM Parameter Store
chunks.content:
When to choose AWS Secrets Manager vs SSM Parameter Store

Both store encrypted values via KMS. Secrets Manager adds: native rotation Lambdas, replication across regions, cross-account resource policies, and is purpose-built for secrets at $0.40/secret/month. SSM Parameter Store SecureString is free for standard parameters and is the right choice for non-rotated config values that happen to be sensitive (third-party API keys, feature flags). Use Secrets Manager for credentials with rotation, Parameter Store for static sensitive config.

Decision rules:
- USE Secrets Manager for: RDS credentials (native rotation), third-party API tokens that need rotation, multi-region replication needs
- USE SSM Parameter Store SecureString for: static API keys, configuration values, environment-specific endpoints
- ENCRYPT both with a customer-managed KMS key (CMK) — not the AWS-managed `aws/secretsmanager` or `aws/ssm` keys — gives you key policies and rotation control
- RESTRICT secret access via resource policies + IAM — `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` should be scoped to specific ARNs and conditions
- ENABLE rotation on RDS secrets — Secrets Manager has built-in rotation Lambdas for RDS, DocumentDB, Redshift

Trade-offs:
- Secrets Manager: rotation built-in vs $0.40/secret/month adds up at scale
- Parameter Store SecureString: free vs no native rotation, no replication
- Customer-managed KMS key: full control vs $1/key/month and operational responsibility

Anti-patterns:
- Storing every config value in Secrets Manager — costs explode and most config values are not secrets
- Storing rotation-needed credentials in Parameter Store — manual rotation rarely happens
- Using the AWS-managed KMS key for production secrets — cannot scope key policy to specific principals

chunks.title: Syncing AWS Secrets Manager into Kubernetes Secrets with External Secrets Operator
chunks.content:
Syncing AWS Secrets Manager into Kubernetes Secrets with External Secrets Operator

External Secrets Operator (ESO) is the production pattern for Kubernetes secrets on AWS. ESO runs in the cluster with an IRSA-bound role that grants `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on specific ARNs. ExternalSecret resources declare 'pull this Secrets Manager secret into a Kubernetes Secret with this name'. ESO refreshes on a configurable interval and updates the K8s Secret in place. Pods consume the K8s Secret via volume mount or env. This avoids static credentials in YAML, supports rotation, and keeps the source of truth in AWS.

Decision rules:
- DEPLOY External Secrets Operator with an IRSA role scoped to specific Secrets Manager ARNs — never `Resource: "*"`
- WRITE one ExternalSecret per logical secret bundle — keep blast radius per ServiceAccount tight
- USE `refreshInterval: 1h` as default — shorter for high-rotation secrets, longer for static
- MOUNT secrets as files (volume) rather than env vars where possible — easier reload on rotation, less leakage via process listing
- PAIR with a sidecar or library that watches the file for changes and reloads — avoids pod restart on every rotation

Trade-offs:
- ESO: clean GitOps story vs another operator to run (lightweight, but a dependency)
- Volume mount vs env: volume reloads on change, env requires pod restart — mount when supported
- Refresh interval: shorter is more responsive but more API calls and higher AWS bill

Anti-patterns:
- Granting ESO `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on `*` — one operator with full secret access defeats segmentation
- Plain Kubernetes Secrets created by humans with `kubectl create secret generic --from-literal` — drift from AWS source of truth, no audit
- Storing ESO IAM keys in a Kubernetes Secret — IRSA is the right pattern

chunks.title: When Vault is the right choice and what its differentiators are
chunks.content:
When Vault is the right choice and what its differentiators are

Vault adds capabilities beyond cloud-native secret stores: dynamic secrets (generate ephemeral DB credentials per request, automatically revoked), PKI engine (issue short-lived TLS certs), Transit engine (encryption-as-a-service without exposing the key), and identity-broker patterns (Vault Agent injects secrets into pods via init container). Choose Vault when: multi-cloud, dynamic credentials are the primary need, or you need a unified secrets platform across very heterogeneous workloads.

Decision rules:
- USE Vault when: multi-cloud workloads, need dynamic database credentials, or need PKI for internal mTLS at scale
- AVOID Vault if AWS-only and Secrets Manager covers your use cases — operational cost is non-trivial
- RUN Vault HA mode (3 or 5 nodes, integrated Raft storage) with auto-unseal via cloud KMS
- AUTHENTICATE workloads to Vault via cloud IAM (AWS IAM auth method, Kubernetes auth method) — never static tokens
- USE Vault Agent or CSI Provider to inject secrets into pods — avoid app-level Vault SDK calls where possible

Trade-offs:
- Vault: most powerful secrets/identity platform vs significant ops investment
- Self-hosted vs HCP Vault: control vs managed — HCP eliminates ops at a cost premium
- Dynamic DB credentials: highest security (per-request lifetime) vs DB connection-pool friction

Anti-patterns:
- Single-node Vault in production — sealing the vault during an incident is a disaster
- Static root tokens checked into infra Git — root token should be sharded (Shamir) and never used after init
- Treating Vault as a glorified KV store — using none of its dynamic-secret or PKI capabilities means you are paying ops cost for no benefit

chunks.title: Credential rotation: scheduled, on-event, and zero-downtime patterns
chunks.content:
Credential rotation: scheduled, on-event, and zero-downtime patterns

Rotation reduces the value of a stolen credential by limiting its useful lifetime. Three rotation triggers: scheduled (e.g. every 90 days), on-event (employee leaves, compromise suspected), and continuous (dynamic secrets — minutes to hours). Zero-downtime rotation requires the application to support two valid credentials simultaneously during the cutover, or to reload secrets without restart. Database credentials use the 'two-user alternation' pattern: rotate user A while app uses user B, switch, rotate user B.

Decision rules:
- ROTATE static credentials at most every 90 days; preferably move them to dynamic credentials with hour-scale lifetimes
- USE the two-user alternation pattern for RDS — Secrets Manager native rotation supports this directly
- ENSURE applications reload secrets without restart — file-watch on mounted secret, SIGHUP handler, or sidecar reload
- ROTATE IMMEDIATELY on: personnel departure with access, suspected compromise, accidental exposure (commit, log, screenshot)
- TEST rotation in staging — rotation that has never been tested fails at the worst time

Trade-offs:
- Frequent rotation: smaller compromise window vs more change risk and operational toil
- Two-user alternation: zero downtime vs requires DB user management and double the IAM/credential mgmt
- Dynamic secrets: best security vs application/library support is uneven

Anti-patterns:
- Quarterly rotation that requires service downtime — teams skip it
- 'Rotation' that just generates a new value without invalidating the old one — old credential is still valid
- Manual rotation runbook — humans forget, automate it

metadata.title: Credential rotation: scheduled, on-event, and zero-downtime patterns
